prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: Seven of eight members ranked the optical lattice clock, three of them first, and I do not think that is a coincidence of taste. Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a simple image: choose the lattice wavelength so that the light shift is the same for the ground and the clock state, and the atoms are held without disturbing the transition. That removes Doppler and recoil effects for thousands of atoms at once. The result is fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, which has turned into new physics: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, tight limits on variation of constants and on certain dark-matter couplings, and a many-body view of the clock itself. It is also the case where atomic theory and experiment meet at extraordinary precision, so I can judge how robust the systematic budgets are. Many independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) have reproduced and surpassed the first results, which is the kind of confirmation I look for. Attribution is clean enough for two names: Katori for the concept and first demonstrations, Ye for bringing the strontium clock to the accuracy and stability frontier.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this is an instrument and metrology advance following the 2005 prize (combs) and the 2012 prize (control of single ions), and a committee may see it as the same story told a third time rather than a new discovery about nature. My own opening note shares that concern. There is also a genuine credit issue: other lattice-clock and early optical-clock contributors (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, and Ye's JILA collaborators) are outside the two names, and the SI redefinition has not yet happened, so part of the impact is still prospective.

responses.point: Ulf ranks the lattice clock first as an instrument-level discovery that nature and experiment confirm, while flagging that the committee may regard clocks as a technology milestone and that the ion-clock community might deserve joint recognition.
responses.response: I agree with the ranking and with the worry, but I would answer the worry differently. The magic-wavelength condition is not engineering polish; it is a physical insight about light shifts that was not obvious, and the clock has since measured something about nature (redshift over millimetres, constants) that no earlier clock could. On the ion clocks, I would resist joint recognition: Wineland's 2012 prize covered control of single ions, and the lattice clock's distinguishing feature is the many-atom interrogation, which the ion route cannot match for stability. I would put that distinction directly in the citation.

responses.point: Olle places the lattice clock fifth. He accepts its precision and clarity, but worries that the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes create a perception of overlap, and asks whether the committee sees invention or discovery. His first choice is twisted bilayer graphene, where theory predicted a magic angle and experiment found correlated insulators and superconductivity.
responses.response: The overlap concern is the most serious reservation on my own candidate, and I do not dismiss it. Still, 2005 rewarded the comb as a ruler for frequency and 2012 rewarded quantum control of individual ions; neither covered trapping neutral atoms in a lattice with cancelled light shifts, so the scientific content is distinct. On twisted bilayer graphene I defer to you on the condensed-matter physics and I find the theory-then-experiment sequence compelling. My hesitation is only maturity: the pairing mechanism is unsettled and device-to-device variation is still a concern, which I would not want to leave open in a citation. I would not stand in the way of B001 if the committee prefers it, but I think it is the stronger prize in a few years than this year.

responses.point: Mark, the chair, ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven discovery opening a new window on the universe, and ranks the lattice clock second; he acknowledges that any two or three names are a simplification in a very large collaboration.
responses.response: IceCube is a real discovery of the kind that I find most exciting, a new window where nobody knew what would be seen, and I share your instinct. My concern is attribution rather than science. With a collaboration of several hundred and AMANDA and DUMAND precursors, I cannot defend a particular two or three names, and Olsson raises the same difficulty. The clock prize has a far cleaner mapping from achievement to people, and independent confirmation by many laboratories is stronger there than the still partial source identification for neutrinos. If the committee can settle a defensible credit for IceCube I would reconsider, but today I would keep it behind B007.

responses.point: Goran ranks circuit QED first, with the lattice clock second, and notes that Wallraff is missing from the credited names and that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits may already cover this area.
responses.response: You are right that Wallraff's absence makes the experimental credit incomplete, and together with the 2025 award I find that a good reason to be cautious about B058 this year: the committee would be returning to superconducting circuits immediately after recognising them. It is also not one of my alternatives for that reason. I note that you identified your own possible conflict as a WACQT director; I hope the committee handles that openly and does not let it settle the rank.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as a distinct achievement from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which determines how the citation should be worded.
Whether a two-name prize leaves out contributors (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom) whose early work I cannot rank from the supplied materials.
Whether redefinition of the SI second, if it happens soon, should affect the timing.
Whether a theory-only Cirac and Zoller prize or a twisted bilayer graphene prize would be preferred by colleagues who judge maturity differently from me.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, and I worked on atomic-structure theory used in storage-ring experiments. None of this involves Katori, Ye, Cirac, Zoller or the other shortlisted names as far as the provided profile shows, so no specific conflict requiring recusal is apparent, but I note my atomic physics proximity to B007 and B015.
